div.p: The maned wolf is the largest South American canid, and in Brazil, its distribution is closely associated with the Cerrado, one of the most threatened biomes in the world. Although the Cerrado have few, small, and often isolated protected areas, these fragments are crucial for the persistence of wide-ranging mammals, providing protection and resources, and facilitating their dispersal movements, especially in areas of intense human activity. Here, we estimated the minimum population size and genetic diversity of maned wolves inhabiting one of the last refuges of Cerrado vegetation in S ã o Paulo State, the most developed, industrialized, and populous state of Brazil. Through fecal DNA analysis of five microsatellite loci, during a 13-month sampling period, we identified 13 maned wolves and observed a genetic diversity similar to other studies conducted in larger and better preserved areas of the central region of the country. However, unlike those studies, we found evidence of inbreeding, deviations from Hardy-Weinberg expectations, and a larger number of animals in relation to the sampled area, thus providing evidence that the population may be threatened.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Large wide-ranging mammals require large areas in which to live; however, the increases in human activities in recent centuries have been reducing the natural areas available for these animals ( Schipper et al. 2008 ). In disturbed landscapes, protected areas are not always sufficiently large to maintain viable populations ( Soul é and Sanjayan 1998 , Laurance et al. 2012 ), although the value of these areas for protection is unquestionable, both as a source of resources and for allowing successful movements during the dispersal behavior of these species.

The Cerrado is the second largest Brazilian biome, occupying 21% of the country ' s territory, and possesses high levels of species richness and endemism ( Silva and Bates 2002 ). However, in the last 35 years, > 50% of its extent has been transformed into pasture and agricultural lands ( Klink and Machado 2005 ). Only 2.2% of the Cerrado area is under legal protection ( Klink and Machado 2005 ), thus leaving wide-ranging species that exceed the limits of protected areas exposed to threats such as hunting, disease, road kill, or scarcity of resources.

The maned wolf ( Chrysocyon brachyurus , Illiger 1815) is the largest South American canid, and in Brazil, its distribution is closely related to the extent of the Cerrado ( Rodden et al. 2004 ). Despite its generalist habits ( Dietz 1984, Motta-Junior et al. 1996, Santos et al. 2003, Massara et al. 2012 ), this species is considered " Near Threatened " by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and its long-term viability may be compromised in some localities as a consequence of intensive habitat degradation ( IUCN 2012 ). The population trends of C. brachyurus are unknown throughout its distribution ( IUCN 2012 ). Maned wolves are solitary canids that form pairs during reproductive periods ( Rodden et al. 2004( Rodden et al. , J á como et al. 2009 ) ). They are territorial, with the couple sharing the same home range, and with little or no overlap areas between neighboring pairs being observed ( Dietz 1984( Dietz , J á como et al. 2009 ) ). Their home range size varies from 30 km 2 ( Dietz 1984 ) to 75 km 2 ( Carvalho and Vasconcellos 1995 ).

The central area of S ã o Paulo, southeastern Brazil, is located at the southeastern limit of the Cerrado extension. This region has been particularly severely deforested over the past two centuries ( Dean 1996, Brito 1997 ); however, despite this major landscape transformation, maned wolves are still found in the area ( Bueno et al. 2003, Lyra-Jorge et al. 2008 ). The area currently contains a few large and many small fragments of Cerrado, most of which are not connected to each other ( Rodrigues andBononi 2008 , Ribeiro et al. 2009 ) and are immersed in an agricultural and urbanized matrix. Few remnants are under legal protection ( Rodrigues and Bononi 2008 ), and all of them are most likely too small to maintain viable long-term maned wolf populations.

Under this scenario, designing conservation strategies, and the prediction of maned wolf population trends require basic knowledge of the genetics, ecology, behavior, and landscape use of this threatened species, which are aspects that are still poorly investigated ( Silveira et al. 2009, IUCN 2012 ), particularly in severely disturbed landscapes ( Massara et al. 2012 ). Thus, we investigated the minimum population size and genetic diversity of maned wolves inhabiting one of the last refuges of Cerrado vegetation in the central area of the S ã o Paulo State, applying a non-invasive sampling method and performing fecal DNA analyses. This information may represent useful tools to monitor the population and the species conservation status over the years, contributing to its maintenance in this landscape that is highly modified by human activities.

div.head: Study area
div.p: The study area was located in the Lu í s Ant ô nio municipality, in the northeast region of S ã o Paulo State ( Figure 1 ). This region is a transition zone between Cerrado and semideciduous vegetation and includes a protected area, the Jata í Ecological Station (JES; 21 ° 35 ′ S-47 ° 48 ′ W), which covers 9010 ha and represents the largest protected area in the state with continuous Cerrado vegetation. This area is surrounded by sugarcane crops, cattle ranches, eucalyptus plantations, dirt roads, and highways.

div.head: Sample collection
div.p: Between October 2008 and December 2009, we conducted 2-day field expeditions once per month inside and surrounding the JES. This protected area is intersected by dirt roads throughout its extent. Therefore, during each expedition, we looked for feces on the dirt roads inside and surrounding the JES, covering approximately 200 km of roads. All of the fieldwork was conducted by two researchers. On the basis of tracks and feces diameter/ morphology ( Dalponte 1997, Chame 2003 ), we collected 41 distinct maned wolf fecal samples and recorded the coordinates of all collection points using a Global Positioning System. The samples were stored in sterile preservativefree plastic tubes without any preservative solution and were kept at -22 ° C in the laboratory until DNA extraction was performed.

div.head: DNA extraction
div.p: We extracted fecal DNA using either the QIAmp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, GmBH, Hilden, Germany) or PSP Spin Stool DNA Kit (Invitek, Regensburg, Germany), according to the manufacturer ' s recommendations. For the extraction of blood DNA to be used as reference sequences in the genetic analysis, we followed the phenol/chloroform/ isoamylic alcohol protocol proposed by Sambrook et al. (1989) . Blood samples (two) were kindly provided by the Americana Municipality Zoo and CENAP/IBAMA.

div.head: Fecal sample individualization and genetic analyses
div.p: To individualize each fecal sample, we amplified a set of seven tetranucleotide microsatellite loci with primers that were initially designed by Francisco et al. (1996) for Canis familiaris (Linnaeus 1758) and successfully characterized for Chrysocyon brachyurus by Fontoura- Rodrigues et al. (2008Rodrigues et al. ( ) : loci 2001Rodrigues et al. ( , 2018Rodrigues et al. ( , 2054Rodrigues et al. ( , 2088Rodrigues et al. ( , 2132Rodrigues et al. ( , 2137Rodrigues et al. ( , and 2140. PCR was performed using a three-primer labeling system ( Schuelke 2000 ). Each amplification (15 μ l) included 7.5 μ l of GoTaq Master Mix (Promega; 1 × buffer, 1.5 m m MgCl 2 , 0.2 m m dNTPs, and 1u Taq polymerase ), 8 pmol of the reverse primer, 2 pmol of the forward primer, 8 pmol of the M13 sequence tagged with the 6-FAM fluorophore, and 150 μ g/ml of bovine serum albumin. The remaining volume of the 15 μ l reaction consisted of the sample DNA. We performed the amplifications in a PTC-100 Thermocycler (MJ Research Inc.), according to the following program (for all We genotyped homozygous samples in three to five independent PCR assays and heterozygous samples two times to prevent genotyping errors that are frequently associated with non-invasive genetic analyses ( Taberlet et al. 1996 ). Only samples that were successfully genotyped for at least five loci were included in the fecal individualization analysis, and only loci that were genotyped for at least 70% of the samples were included in the analyses.

We conducted individual identification of genotypes with Gimlet version 1.3.3 ( Vali è re 2002 ). We determined the probability of identity (p (ID) ), i.e., the probability of two individuals in the population randomly sharing identical genotypes for all of the analyzed loci ( Paetkau et al. 1998, Waits et al. 2001 ), to quantify the discriminatory power of the microsatellite dataset among all of the individualized samples. The p (ID) values were calculated for each locus using Gimlet and then multiplied among the loci to obtain the total p (ID) ( Paetkau et al. 1998 ). We also estimated the probability of identity assuming siblings (p (ID)sib ) ( Waits et al. 2001 ).

We determined the total and per-locus genotyping error rates (allelic dropout) by dividing the number of detected errors by the number of cases in which an error might have been detected (i.e., the total number of heterozygous genotyping reactions; see Broquet and Petit 2004 ). We investigated the occurrence of null alleles with Micro-Checker 2.2.3 ( Van Oosterhout et al. 2004 ). We used Genepop 3.4 ( Raymond and Rousset 1995 ) to estimate the expected (H E ) and observed (H O ) heterozygosity, and to test each locus for linkage disequilibrium and deviations from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) proportions (Markov chain exact test; Guo and Thompson 1992 ), with all of these analyses including 10,000 dememorizations, 1000 batches, and 10,000 interactions per batch. Using FStat 2.9.3 ( Goudet 1995 ), we estimated the allelic richness and the F IS coefficient ( Weir and Cockerham 1984 ) as a measure of the inbreeding level in the population.

Bottleneck 1.2.02 ( Piry et al. 1999 ) was used to test heterozygosity excess as a consequence of a recent bottleneck event using a " Wilcoxon test " . We assumed a two-phase mutation model incorporating 10%, 20%, and 30% of infinite allele mutation model (IAM), with 10,000 iterations. The test was also repeated assuming IAM and the stepwise mutation model.

We estimated the genetic relationships between individualized maned wolves using ML-Relate ( Kalinowski et al. 2006 ). The maximum likelihood estimate of relatedness (r) ( Blouin 2003 ) was employed to discriminate four common pedigree relationships: unrelated (U), half siblings (HS), full siblings (FS), and parent-offspring (PO). When the estimated putative relationships between individual pairs differed from unrelated relationships, we used the same software to assess the uncertainty (p-values) of these estimates by testing two a priori hypotheses: a putative relationship with a higher likelihood (HS, FS, or PO) against an alternative hypothesis (the " unrelated " relationship). When the pair comparisons exhibited a low p-value ( < 0.05), we excluded the alternative hypothesis and accepted the relationship with the maximum likelihood (HS, FS, or PO). Because we had no control group of samples with known relationships to calibrate the analysis, the goal of this analysis was to verify the existence of related animals in the study area, rather than defining exact categories of kinship.

div.head: Discrimination of individuals and genetic variability
div.p: We successfully extracted DNA from and genotyped the 41 collected samples. Of the seven microsatellite loci that were initially tested, only five displayed an amplification success > 70%; therefore, we excluded loci 2132 and 2137 from further analyses. Among the 41 fecal samples, we identified 13 distinct maned wolves (Figure 1), and 9 (69.2%) of these individuals were sampled at least twice. The probability of identity estimated for the five analyzed loci indicated that our microsatellite panel was efficient in discriminating individuals within the entire dataset (p (ID) = 0.1 × 10 -19 and p (ID)sib = 0.8 × 10 -6 ). Values < 0.001 may be considered satisfactory ( Waits et al. 2001 ). The observed allelic frequencies for the seven analyzed loci are presented in Table 1 . Our data displayed no evidence of null alleles.

Genetic variability analysis indicated mean values of 0.52 and 0.72 for H O and H E , respectively. The number of alleles per locus ranged from 3 (locus 2088) to 8 (locus 2140), with a mean of 5.4 alleles per locus. The range size, number of alleles, allelic richness, observed and expected heterozygosity, and allelic dropout rates for the analyzed loci are presented in Table 2 .

No linkage disequilibrium was detected among the seven analyzed loci; however, we observed significant deviations from the HWE for two loci (2054 and 2140; Bonferroni correction p < 0.00714) ( Table 3 ). The estimated total F IS coefficient was significant (F IS = 0.324; p < 0.01), indicating a heterozygote deficit in the sampled population.

Testing for the recent occurrence of a bottleneck event in this maned wolf population resulted in no significant values based on all of the tested mutation models. Investigation of the patterns of the genetic relationships between all possible pair combinations indicated significant r values for the PO, FS, and HS pedigree categories (p < 0.05), which reveals the existence of related individuals in the protected area. Theoretically, the r values for the FS and PO relationships are distributed around a mean of 0.5, and those for HS around a mean of 0.25 ( Blouin et al. 1996 ). The significant values of r ranged from 0.000 to 0.5253.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Both estimated values for the probability of identity (p (ID)unbiased of 0.159 × 10 -19 and p (ID)sib of 0.8 × 10 -6 ) are considered satisfactory for individual identification in non-invasive genotyping ( Waits et al. 2001 ) and indicate that the analyzed loci successfully distinguished each individual, even in the presence of closely related animals in the study area.

Mainly owing to low DNA quality and quantity, microsatellite analyses of non-invasively collected samples, including feces, are commonly affected by genotyping errors, such as allelic dropout or false allele amplification, and individual sample identification and population size estimates could consequently be biased ( Taberlet et al. 1996, Waits et al. 2001, Broquet and Petit 2004, Prugh et al. 2005 ). Consistent genotypes were successfully obtained here as a result of a careful analysis based on three established conditions: (i) we genotyped heterozygotes twice and confirmed the genotypes of homozygotes in three to five independent PCR assays; (ii) we included a locus in our analysis only if > 70% of samples were successfully genotyped for that locus; and (iii) in the final analysis, we only included those samples that were genotyped for at least 70% of the analyzed loci. Following these rules, we had to exclude two loci from analyses (2132 and 2137), although we were still able to successfully distinguish the animals in the study area. We emphasize that even with a careful analysis of each distinct individual identified, results should be considered with caution, as population size overestimation may occur in studies based on low-quality fecal DNA samples ( Taberlet et al. 1996, Waits et al. 2001 ).

We detected a population of 13 maned wolves inside the protected area. In the recent past, 26 animals were genetically sampled within the JES and surrounding municipalities, during approximately 7 years of trapping ( Mattos 2003 ). The high efficiency of the non-invasive method employed here is therefore remarkable, as we were able to account for half of the number of maned wolves identified in the former study, only within the JES area, in approximately 15% of the time. The application of mark-recapture models for this population could generate a more robust population size estimate; however, the unsystematic feces collection method employed here and the long sampling period (13 months) were not appropriate to generate such models. Nevertheless, the high number of replicates we collected may support an actual estimate of the minimum population size in the JES.

Previous estimates of maned wolf densities in Cerrado areas from central Brazil have revealed that the species occurs in low densities in preserved areas [ ± 5.19/100 km 2 ( Silveira et al. 2009 ) and ± 3.64/100 km 2 ( Trolle et al. 2007 )]. Although we did not obtain a density estimate here, our population size estimate within the JES area ( ∼ 100 km 2 ) is much higher compared with the earlier studies. Although maned wolves occur in monogamous breeding pairs inhabiting exclusive territories ( Dietz 1984 ), our findings support the idea that these animals may be more concentrated inside the reserve, tolerating greater overlapping territories than usual. A similar trend was observed for pumas within the same protected area, and the JES apparently holds a larger number of pumas than other recorded areas ( Miotto et al. 2012( Miotto et al. , 2014 ). In the central area of Brazil, where the natural Cerrado vegetation is being successively replaced by agricultural uses ( Klink and Machado 2005 ), it has been established that maned wolves may use the matrix continuously ( Trolle et al. 2007, Silveira et al. 2009, Vynne et al. 2011 ), as open areas favor this species. This behavior certainly occurs in our study area. However, the surroundings of JES are becoming more urbanized over the years and, consequently, more inhospitable to the movements of large mammals such as pumas and maned wolves.

The number and range size of alleles assessed here were similar to those reported by Fontoura-Rodrigues et al. ( 2008) , although we observed range size extensions for loci 2088 and 2001. Three of the analyzed loci (2132, 2054, and 2088) were also examined by Lion et al. (2011) in the central area of Brazil in the Distrito Federal, facilitating comparisons throughout the species ' distribution. These authors also found a higher rate of errors in the amplification of locus 2132, although they did not exclude it from their analysis as in the present work.

The genetic variation we observed (H E = 0.72) was similar to the values estimated by Lion et al. (2011) (H E = 0.71) and Fontoura- Rodrigues et al. (2008) (H E = 0.75). The deviations from the HWE proportions observed for two of the analyzed loci (2054 and 2140) may be related to a number of causes. However, there was no evidence of null alleles, a Wahlund effect, or the occurrence of a recent bottleneck found in our data. Thus, such HWE deviations could be associated with inbreeding, in agreement with the observed heterozygote deficit (F IS > 0), although the low number of analyzed loci or sampled animals could also be influencing the deviations. One factor that could be contributing to this phenomenon is the isolation of the JES within the region, as the nearest preserved areas are approximately 100 km away and the matrix is inhospitable to maned wolves. The landscape where the JES is emerged has been severely transformed, especially in the last century ( Dean 1996 ). The expansion of urban centers, the extensive conversion of ranches and native forest fragments into sugarcane crops and eucalyptus or citrus plantations, and the implementation of a large road network connecting municipalities have drastically reduced natural habitats, which in turn may likely have reduced the maned wolf population size over the years.

In fact, when studying the same population, Mattos (2003) reported the death of several individuals in the vicinity of the JES due to car collisions or by hunting. The continuous removal of individuals and the difficulty of new animals entering in the population over time may be generating impacts on genetic variation, resulting in more evident signs of inbreeding. Inbreeding is a typical problem of closed and small populations with important conservation implications, as it has consequences for reproduction and reproductive vigor, increasing the risk of extinction ( Frankham et al. 2002 ). The presence of domestic animals within the area must also be considered as the environment becomes urbanized, because they may compete with, prey upon, or introduce diseases into the population ( Rodden et al. 2004, Lacerda et al. 2009, Curi et al. 2010 ). Thus, the existence of the JES alone will most likely not be sufficient for the conservation of maned wolves in the region ( Putz et al. 2001 ), and their ability to explore surrounding fragments of natural habits and to move across the matrix will serve as a determinant of their persistence ( Fahrig 2003 ). Among mammals, wide-ranging species such as the maned wolf are at the top of extinction risk ( Cardillo et al. 2008 ), and in developed areas, implementing management actions at the landscape level is imperative. Monitoring population parameters over the years and predicting their trends are important tools for planning the future of the species in the central region of the state.
